source.title: From Unimodal to Multimodal: Scaling up Projectors to Align Modalities
source.authors: Mayug Maniparambil; Raiymbek Akshulakov; Yasser Abdelaziz Dahou Djilali; Sanath Narayan; Ankit Singh; Noel E. O'Connor

record.tranche_reason: It tests whether frozen vision and language representations can be aligned by learned projectors, a different method for assessing interchangeable representations than the original studies’ similarity analyses.
record.gate_note: The paper reports many downstream classification, localization, multilingual, and retrieval results. Rows below retain results that directly assess projector-based cross-modal alignment, its relation to CKA, or how alignment performance changes with training data. Results cited from other work are not included.
record.test_reason: The study tests whether frozen, independently trained vision and text encoders can be mapped into a shared space by lightweight projectors. It checks whether CKA predicts how easily they align (toy linear-map loss, 45 real pairs, many encoder-pair ablations). It compares the projector-aligned pair against end-to-end CLIP. That bears on V4 (interchangeable representations), using a different method from the originals' similarity analyses. It is also largely a method paper, so much of its output is downstream benchmark performance.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that semantically similar frozen unimodal encoders can be aligned with lightweight projectors. This gives CLIP-level or better performance (76.3% ImageNet) with about 20× less paired data and 65× less alignment compute. CKA is a good selector of encoder pairs. They also state that unimodal strengths are kept in the joint space. A caveat: the unimodal encoders' own pretraining compute is not counted.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains lightweight nonlinear projectors between frozen unimodal encoders on paired image-caption data, rather than directly testing spontaneous representation convergence or relying on a linear map alone.
record.method_sensitivity: Alignment-task performance varies with the alignment dataset and its concept coverage and image-caption quality. The authors state that linear- and RBF-kernel CKA trends were largely consistent.

fits_no_version.finding: Which unimodal benchmark scores predict cross-modal alignability. STS r=0.72, semantic search r=0.13 (n.s.), average unimodal performance r=0.47 (n.s.), vs CKA r=0.81.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Representational similarity (CKA) predicts cross-modal mappability better than unimodal task performance does.

fits_no_version.finding: In a synthetic latent model, higher CKA between two random nonlinear views of a shared latent lowers the minimum linear-map CLIP loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Similarity of kernel structure bounds the ease of linear contrastive alignment.

record.problems: The main alignment outcomes are downstream task metrics rather than direct measures of representation interchangeability. Projectors are trained on paired image-caption data, so results do not establish spontaneous convergence. The paper reports no uncertainty for most task scores.
record.rows_left_out: Other downstream benchmark results, including classification, segmentation, multilingual evaluation, long-caption retrieval, and projector-architecture ablations, were not included because they do not directly test representation interchangeability beyond the alignment results recorded here.

untested.parts: No test of whether cross-model alignment rises with model size, capability, data or compute. Encoder sizes appear in Fig 4/A.5 but no size trend is reported.

Image-caption alignment is measured (CKA), but not whether it rises as both models improve. A.7 reports that average text-encoder benchmark performance only weakly predicts ease of alignment (r=0.47, p=0.08). This is indirect and not a test of V2.

No unpaired mapping, stitching or relative representations. Linear-only maps are used only in the 500-iteration toy, not as the full alignment. Loss relative to the original unimodal spaces is not quantified beyond downstream task retention.
No interpretable features or circuits examined.
States linear and RBF CKA trends were 'largely consistent' but reports no numbers. No neighbour, input-set or OOD sensitivity of the convergence measure is reported.
No test of whether alignment plateaus or is explained by shared data or objectives.

missing.what: Average unimodal text-model performance vs alignment: Pearson r=0.47, p=0.08, not predictive
Projector-only training of the CLIP encoders vs DINOv2-ARL (72.10 vs 76.45 ImageNet; 59.04 vs 60.14 COCO I2T) and CLIP trained from scratch (50.30)
Alignment performance rises only slowly with more randomly sampled LAION data (to ~160M) and is beaten by the curated 20M set
Projector architecture ablation: identity text-side or MLP-only projectors give 68.8% vs 76.1% ImageNet
Unimodal capabilities (multilingual, long-context, localization) retained after projection

record.verdict_notes: The relation is borderline between T2 and T4, since this is mainly a method paper relying on convergence findings, including PRH (arXiv:2405.07987, an original source). It does run its own tests of CKA vs mappability and of mapping quality, so it is kept as T2 for V4 only. The mapping is nonlinear and needs millions of paired examples, so it is weaker evidence for the 'simple/little-loss' wording of V4. Rows r7–r18 are downstream metrics without a baseline. Their verdict relies on within-table contrasts.

versions.untested_parts: No sweep tests whether independently trained representations become more aligned as model size, capability, data, or compute increase.
The study aligns image and caption representations but does not test whether their alignment rises as both encoders improve.
No comparison of seeds, shared features, or subspaces across same-architecture networks.

The study trains nonlinear projectors with paired image-caption data; it does not test linear-only or unpaired mappings, stitching, relative representations, or preservation of representations with little loss.
No recurring interpretable features or circuits are examined.

It does not test whether convergence itself disappears under different similarity metrics, settings, or out-of-distribution inputs. It reports that linear- and RBF-kernel CKA trends were largely consistent.
It does not test whether incomplete or plateauing alignment is caused by shared data or objectives rather than a common model of reality.

rows.subject: 45 vision-text encoder pairs (five text encoders × nine vision encoders)
rows.stage_stated: pretrained encoders; projector alignment experiment
rows.operation_detail: Measured CKA and CLIP loss after 500 SGD iterations fitting a linear layer.
rows.measure: Relationship between CKA and final CLIP loss, defined as ease of alignment.
rows.value: The text reports a strong inverse relationship: higher CKA corresponded to lower CLIP loss.
rows.note: Aggregate result across the 45 encoder pairs; no coefficient is given in the text.
rows.check: Shows that linear-map CLIP loss after 500 SGD steps varies strongly across the 45 pairs, tracking CKA. Some pairs map easily and others do not, so 'little loss' holds only for high-CKA pairs. No coefficient or loss values are given in the text.

rows.subject: 1,000 randomly generated latent-model A/B pairs
rows.size_stated: Each A and B contains 32 vectors of 16 dimensions
rows.stage_stated: synthetic toy experiment
rows.operation_detail: Compared CKA with minimum CLIP loss after fitting a linear transformation.

conditions.value: Independent random nonlinear transformations of shared latent Z with additive noise

rows.measure: Relationship between CKA and minimum CLIP loss.
rows.value: The text reports a clear negative correlation: minimum CLIP loss decreased as CKA increased.
rows.note: Synthetic setting; no correlation coefficient is stated.
rows.check: Synthetic random-latent toy (32×16 random matrices), not trained models. It does not measure what V4 names in real systems. Also, 10^3 instances is likely extracted as '1,000', which is fine.

rows.subject: DINOv2 and text-encoder pairs
rows.size_stated: DINOv2 variants include Tiny through Giant; text encoder sizes not stated
rows.stage_stated: pretrained encoders with trained projectors
rows.operation_detail: Compared encoder-pair CKA with Flickr30k retrieval performance after projector training.
rows.measure: Pearson correlation between CKA and retrieval performance.
rows.note: Aggregate correlation across the encoder-pair ablation; the paper says both image and text retrieval correlate strongly with CKA.
rows.check: Correlation (r=0.92) between CKA and post-projector Flickr30k retrieval. It shows mapping quality depends on the encoder pair rather than holding uniformly. The subject spans multiple vision encoders (DINOv2, ViT-AugReg, ConvNeXT), not only DINOv2.

source_check.correct: Pearson correlation = 0.92 across multiple vision-encoder families and text encoders, including DINOv2, ViT-AugReg and ConvNeXT. The extracted caption prints p = 2.1e7; p = 2.1e-7 cannot be verified from this text.

source_check.problem: The subject excludes non-DINOv2 vision encoders, and the reported uncertainty silently repairs a malformed exponent.

source_check.notes: The supplied text is arXiv v2, dated March 2025, titled Harnessing Frozen Unimodal Encoders for Flexible Multimodal Alignment. Its Figure A.5 p-value is malformed; other needed results are readable. Retrieval supports practical alignment rather than direct representation equivalence; compute savings exclude unimodal pretraining.
